analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers sell individual plans nationwide under the rules of whichever state they choose.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let a health insurer selling individual health plans pick one state — its 'primary state' — and follow that state's insurance rules everywhere, exempting it from the laws of every other state where it sells. Insurers could therefore shop for the state with the fewest required benefits, the loosest rate rules, and the weakest consumer protections, and use those rules nationwide. The bill included a bold-print warning to buyers, some limits on raising premiums for people whose health worsens, an outside-appeal process, and a federal floor for insurer reserves, but the core effect was to override state regulation of the individual insurance market [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, which could designate a lightly regulated state as their primary state and escape every other state's mandated-benefit, rate-review, and consumer-protection laws. Healthier individual buyers might see cheaper, skinnier plans on the market [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: An insurer selling individual coverage in any 'secondary' state is exempt from that state's laws governing the offer, sale, rating (including medical underwriting), renewal, and issuance of that coverage, except for a short list of financial-solvency, fraud, claims-practice, and tax requirements [S3].
The insurer's chosen 'primary state' has sole jurisdiction to enforce the laws governing the coverage, even for policies sold to residents of other states [S2] [S3].

The bill's stated findings argue that variations in state law make individual coverage more expensive and impede its sale, which is the rationale insurers offered for one set of rules nationwide [S3].

Cheaper, less-regulated plans would have been available to healthy buyers in states with strong mandated-benefit laws, because those mandates would no longer apply to plans sold under another state's rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions and sicker enrollees, who would remain in state-regulated plans as healthier buyers migrate to cheaper out-of-state coverage, pushing their premiums up. States lose their authority to regulate plans sold to their own residents, and buyers lose the benefit mandates and rate protections of their home state — the bill itself requires a notice warning that the policy 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' of the buyer's state [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's own required disclosure tells buyers the policy may be cheaper because it is not subject to their state's mandated benefits or its consumer protection and rate-change laws — meaning the cheaper price comes partly from stripped-down coverage [S3].

Allowing insurers to operate under the least-regulated state's rules would draw healthier people into cheap narrow plans and leave sicker, costlier people in state-regulated plans, raising premiums for those who can least afford it; the bill directs the Comptroller General to study exactly this effect on the number of uninsured and underinsured and on the availability and cost of coverage for people with pre-existing conditions [S3].

Enforcement is split: a secondary state's remedies are limited to a short list — solvency exams, fraud, unfair claims practices, insolvency-guaranty participation, and independent review — and courts reviewing a secondary state's challenge must apply the primary state's laws [S3].

The bill permits medical underwriting (health-based rating) at initial sale, so the protections against re-rating apply only at renewal, and insurers can still raise premiums for an entire class based on claims experience [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued one set of rules would cut compliance costs and premiums in the individual market. The cost falls on the buyers with the least bargaining power: coverage sold under another state's rules can omit the benefits, rate protections, and consumer safeguards of the buyer's home state — the bill says so in its own mandatory notice — and the drain of healthier buyers into those plans would push up premiums for people with pre-existing conditions, an effect the bill itself ordered studied. The consumer safeguards in the bill (external review, a solvency floor, a ban on re-rating at renewal) are narrow compared with the scope of state law it overrides.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jim DeMint introduced the Health Care Choice Act of 2007 on December 13, 2007, joined by Republican cosponsors including Senators Coburn, Brownback, Inhofe, Burr, Corker, and Vitter [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators and the state-level consumer protections, benefit mandates, and rate rules that govern individual health plans were left intact. The bill's supporters — insurers seeking a single, lighter regulatory regime — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and existing consumer protections

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would exempt insurers selling individual coverage in other states from those states' insurance laws.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee of referral never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have let insurers designate whichever state's rules they preferred and sell individual plans nationwide under them, escaping every other state's mandated benefits, rate restrictions, and consumer-protection laws. Insurers profit from selling thinner plans, so their gain in this bill runs against the interests of buyers and of states' ability to set coverage standards.

States would have lost jurisdiction over plans sold to their residents: the primary state alone could enforce the governing laws, and secondary states' enforcement was limited to a short list of solvency, fraud, and claims-practice matters.
